- Fable is exceptional at drawing. It’s ability to render an image with JavaScript actually has me questioning the value of dedicated image models. I prefer the images I’ve gotten fable/opus to make for me over those from gpt-image, it’s wild to think we’re at this point.

comments.author: xp84
comments.text:
This is interesting. For a long time it was pointed out that ZIP codes, unlike say, city or state boundaries, were not properly representable as polygons, since they don't divide up acreage into zones, but rather label postal delivery routes. Suppose I build a new neighborhood way out in the middle of nowhere. The "polygon" concept suggests that we could look and see what polygon I'm in, and that will determine what post office delivers my mail. But in reality, if there was no route to that area already, they could decide to make it part of any one of the surrounding routes.
I suppose though, as long as you let the polygons map has uncontained areas, where no routes currently exist, it's a doable task to draw polygons around the limits of every route network, as long as you don't mind that they may have lots of weird ragged edges.

comments.author: jlhawn
comments.text:
I wonder if this could be used anywhere as an alternative to Lloyd's algorithm. I have a hobby project which uses Lloyd's to "relax" an icosohedral equal area mesh on the surface of a sphere [1]. I'm going to try to swap it out with an adaptation of this and see if it's much better or if I can afford more iterations with this method.
Edit: tried it, and it’s definitely
not
better for this use case. e-means wins by needing fewer passes over a huge dataset, but relaxing a mesh on a sphere has no dataset: each Voronoi cell’s centroid can be computed directly from its geometry. Mini-batches just swap that for a noisy sampled estimate of the same thing. It has the same objective and the same optimum, so at best it matches Lloyd. In practice it was much slower and left the grid noisy, and with small sample budgets it even tangled the mesh.

This is the real fear. We had a flood of engineers who entered the profession in the past 10-15 years who were decidedly average. Just show up, their PM assigns them a ticket to make a widget with a button, they use their TypeScript bootcamp skills to code up a widget with a button, ticket moved to In Review, job's done.

comments.author: saulpw
comments.text:
I'm a fan of the 'sandwich' model: someone needs to say what to do, someone needs to do it, and someone needs to say if it's been done [well enough].  Even if AI can do that middle bit entirely, we still need humans at the beginning and the end.  Replace the humans at the start and you have a paperclip-optimizer; replace them at the end and you have slop.
The problem is that software in corporations has typically been product managers at the front, software engineers in the middle, and QA at the end.  Software developers who also have good product sense and do diligent QA are still needed.  Programmers who treated their job as leetcode exercises are not needed anymore.
